scenes.title: REFORMING VIETNAM’S POLITICAL SYSTEM
scenes.subtitle: History of the Communist Party of Vietnam · Topic 6

presenter.script: Good morning. Our topic is reforming Vietnam’s political system. We will use practical examples to explain why reform is necessary.

audience.heading: How can reform make the system work better for its people?
audience.body: Why reform · What changes · Our responsibility

presenter.script: Our central question is simple: how can reform make Vietnam’s political system work better for its people? We will connect historical context, current changes and our responsibilities as students.

audience.heading: Party leadership
audience.body: The Party leads the political system and is also part of it.

presenter.script: The textbook explains that the Party leads the political system and is also part of it. This is our starting point.

audience.heading: Different roles. Shared public purpose.
audience.body: The State manages public affairs under the law.

presenter.script: The State manages public affairs under the law. The Vietnam Fatherland Front and socio-political organisations also have distinct roles. These roles should remain clear when we discuss reform.

audience.heading: The people’s mastery
audience.body: People are the focus of the system’s purpose.

presenter.script: The people exercise their right to mastery. Reform therefore concerns how institutions organise work, coordinate and take responsibility. What happens when these connections become unclear?

audience.heading: Where do I begin?
audience.body: One person. One application. Many connections.

presenter.script: Imagine a person trying to submit one application. They see several offices and several possible routes. They need to know where to begin. This scene is an illustration of a problem, not a record of a real application.

audience.heading: Who takes responsibility?
audience.body: Overlapping steps can make a simple journey difficult.

presenter.script: The red cords represent overlapping procedures, crossing responsibilities and unclear coordination. They do not mean that the whole political system is chaotic. Notice the blocked route. If nobody takes the lead, the citizen may be asked to return or repeat information.

audience.heading: Make the path clearer
audience.body: Clear responsibility. Better coordination.

presenter.script: Let us apply reform. The cords separate and the routes become clearer. This shows the intended direction: clearer tasks and better coordination. The movement is a visual explanation. It is not evidence that a reform has already solved every problem.

audience.heading: Institutions must keep pace
audience.body: Development creates new demands.

presenter.script: Why is reform necessary? First, economic and social development creates new demands. Institutions need the capacity to respond. A structure that once worked may need to change as public needs and economic activity become more complex.

audience.heading: Make responsibility clear
audience.body: Each task needs a lead and effective coordination.

presenter.script: Second, administrative work needs clear responsibility. Resolution 18 calls for one agency to take the main responsibility for each task, while others coordinate. Fewer offices alone do not tell us whether an application becomes easier to complete. A clear lead also gives staff and citizens a place to ask for updates. Coordination remains necessary; the other offices still have duties.

audience.heading: Build the capacity to adapt
audience.body: Clearer structures must work in practice.

presenter.script: Third, deeper international integration raises demands for capable and predictable institutions. These pressures make reform an ongoing task. After the pathways change, we still need to ask: can staff carry out their duties, and can people use the service?

audience.heading: 1986 · Đổi Mới
audience.body: Comprehensive renovation; renewed economic thinking.

presenter.script: In 1986, the Sixth Congress responded to crisis with comprehensive Đổi Mới, or Renovation. It renewed economic thinking while keeping the socialist goal.

audience.heading: 2017 · Organisational renewal
audience.body: Resolution 18: a streamlined, effective and efficient system.

presenter.script: The process continued through Party renewal in 1992 and the 2011 Platform. In 2017, Resolution 18 focused on organisational structure, overlapping functions and responsibility.

audience.heading: 2025 · Local government reform
audience.body: Resolution 60: policy direction for restructuring.

presenter.script: In 2025, Resolution 60 provided direction for a specific local-government change. These milestones have different roles. They are not identical events or a simple chain that proves later reforms successful.

audience.heading: 63 provincial-level units
audience.body: The starting structure.

presenter.script: Here is our main practical example. The model begins with 63 provincial-level units. Its shapes are stylised, so they should not be read as official administrative boundaries.

audience.heading: 34 provincial-level units
audience.body: What changed: the organisation of local government.

presenter.script: The move to 34 units is a verified organisational change. The policy aims to reduce administrative focal points and improve coordination. The animation makes the scale visible; it does not measure the quality of public services.

audience.heading: Province → Commune
audience.body: Two-tier local government operating from 1 July 2025.

presenter.script: The Party Central Committee adopted Resolution 60 in April 2025. The National Assembly then adopted Resolution 202 and Law 72 in June. New local authorities began operating on 1 July, with province and commune levels. The district level ended. Commune-level units include communes, wards and special zones.

audience.heading: What determines success?
audience.body: A smaller structure must deliver in practice.

presenter.script: This gives us three layers: Party direction, a legal framework and implementation. Success depends on capable staff, clear duties, accountability and people’s experience. If citizens still submit the same papers in several places, changing the number of units is not enough. We need evidence about the actual service. A useful assessment asks about repeated submissions, access to help and clarity of responsibility, rather than relying on the new unit count alone.

audience.heading: Enforce
audience.body: Address violations through the applicable rules.

presenter.script: Structure also needs integrity. The Political Report to the 14th National Party Congress calls for prevention and strict handling of violations, with no exceptions. This is a policy principle.

audience.heading: Prevent
audience.body: Reduce opportunities for abuse.

presenter.script: Prevention matters alongside enforcement. Clear duties, supervision and checks can reduce opportunities for abuse. The textbook’s lessons connect institution building with responsibility and control of power.

audience.heading: Disclose
audience.body: Information needs verification and follow-up.

presenter.script: Decree 130 provides an example of asset and income control. Disclosure needs verification and follow-up. Our three labels summarise the discussion; they are not a quotation. Consistent implementation must be assessed through evidence.

scenes.title: The journey continues
scenes.subtitle: DIGITAL SERVICES · People at the centre

audience.heading: Know where to submit
audience.body: Access online, with hands-on help when needed.

presenter.script: Our citizen returns. The first question is practical: where do I submit? An online portal helps only if people can use it. Hands-on support belongs inside the same service journey. The person who cannot use the portal should still have a practical route to complete the task.

audience.heading: Know what happens next
audience.body: Reuse available data where permitted.

presenter.script: Next comes processing. Reusing information where permitted can reduce repeated effort. The illustration does not claim a specific legal procedure or a guaranteed processing time.

audience.heading: Know the status
audience.body: Follow progress and find support.

presenter.script: People also need to follow progress and find help. Hanoi’s plan covers digital public-service skills across 126 communes and wards. The city has also called for mobile digital-literacy support. These are implementation measures, not proof that everyone has received assistance.

audience.heading: Reach a clear outcome
audience.body: An accessible service keeps the whole journey visible.

presenter.script: At the end, the person should know how to receive the result. The 2024 PAPI findings report gaps in digital access before the 2025 restructuring. They remind us to examine different people’s experiences. The lesson of taking the people as the root means asking whether residents can actually use the service.

audience.heading: What can students contribute?
audience.body: From understanding reform to taking responsibility.

presenter.script: We have discussed institutions, responsibility and services. Our role as students begins with how we study these changes, work together and explain them honestly.

scenes.title: Responsibility starts with our work
scenes.subtitle: Topic 6 · Commitments to put into practice

audience.heading: Learn deeply
audience.body: Understand the argument. Check the original source.

presenter.script: Academic responsibility means understanding the argument and checking the source. We should be able to explain why an example supports our conclusion.

audience.heading: Participate
audience.body: Agree on tasks. Complete them. Support one another.

presenter.script: Team responsibility means clear tasks, reliable work and support for others. Actual assignments remain for our members to confirm.

audience.heading: Act with integrity
audience.body: Separate verified facts, goals and interpretations.

presenter.script: Presentation responsibility means answering with evidence and admitting what we do not know. We apply the textbook’s lessons about capability, people’s needs and practical implementation to our own learning.

audience.heading: 2025–26 · Implementation
audience.body: Structural changes are verified; service outcomes need evidence.

presenter.script: The 2025–26 period concerns restructuring and implementation already under way. We distinguish verified changes from results that still need assessment.

audience.heading: 2030 · Development goal
audience.body: Modern industry and upper-middle income.

presenter.script: For 2030, the development goal is modern industry and upper-middle income. Institutions are a means to support development. A future target is not an achieved result.

audience.heading: 2045 · Long-term vision
audience.body: A developed, high-income country.

presenter.script: The 2045 vision is a developed, high-income country. The textbook’s lessons ask us to start from people’s needs and judge practical results. That connects our historical discussion to today. Let us now test these ideas together.

audience.heading: Đổi Mới 1986
audience.body: Raise your hand for A, B, C or D.

presenter.script: Read the question and allow time to think. Ask the class to raise their hands for A, B, C or D in turn. Select the class’s answer, then press Submit. Explain the reasoning briefly. Do not advance until the discussion is finished.

audience.question: By the mid-1980s, Vietnam was in a socio-economic crisis under a centrally planned, subsidised economy. Which decision best matches the Party’s response at the Sixth National Congress in 1986?

options.text: Tighten central planning and subsidies to restore control over production.
Replace the socialist goal with a market model adopted from other countries.
Postpone economic changes until political institutions had been reorganised first.
Renew economic thinking and end the bureaucratic subsidy system, keeping the socialist goal.

assessment.explanation: The Sixth Congress, held in Hanoi on 15–18 December 1986, set out the line of comprehensive Đổi Mới. It called for renewing thinking, starting with economic thinking, and for ending the centrally planned, bureaucratic subsidy mechanism, and it is seen as a turning point in Vietnam’s transition to socialism. This is the starting point for later reforms of the political system; it does not show that any particular later reform has succeeded.

audience.heading: Restructuring
audience.body: Raise your hand for A, B, C or D.

presenter.script: Read the question and allow time to think. Ask the class to raise their hands for A, B, C or D in turn. Select the class’s answer, then press Submit. Explain the reasoning briefly. Do not advance until the discussion is finished.

audience.question: Which description matches the local government model that began operating on 1 July 2025?

options.text: 34 provincial-level units, with province and commune tiers.
63 provincial-level units, with province and commune tiers.
34 provincial-level units, with province, district, and commune tiers.
63 provincial-level units, with province, district, and commune tiers.

assessment.explanation: From 1 July 2025, local government has two tiers: province-level units (provinces and centrally run cities) and commune-level units (communes, wards and special zones), and the district level has ended. The model follows Party Central Committee Resolution 60-NQ/TW of 12 April 2025, and the National Assembly adopted Resolution 202/2025/QH15 on province-level units on 12 June 2025. This is an organizational change; whether services improve needs separate evidence.

audience.heading: People at the center
audience.body: Raise your hand for A, B, C or D.

presenter.script: Read the question and allow time to think. Ask the class to raise their hands for A, B, C or D in turn. Select the class’s answer, then press Submit. Explain the reasoning briefly. Do not advance until the discussion is finished.

audience.question: The Sixth Congress (1986) put “take the people as the root” first among its main lessons. A commune offers online public services, but many older residents cannot complete the forms. Which action best applies this lesson?

options.text: Count the online applications received and treat the total as the measure of success.
Publish a written guide on the portal and ask residents to try again alone.
Provide hands-on help with submitting and show residents how to track progress.
Keep the online process unchanged and refer residents to relatives for help.

assessment.explanation: The Sixth Congress placed taking the people as the root first among its four main lessons, together with building and promoting the working people’s mastery. For public services, this means judging reform by whether residents can actually use and follow them. Hands-on help and progress tracking address the barrier directly; application counts, a written guide or a family referral do not show that it has been removed. A policy calling for such support does not establish that every resident has already received it.

audience.heading: One task, one lead
audience.body: Raise your hand for A, B, C or D.

presenter.script: Read the question and allow time to think. Ask the class to raise their hands for A, B, C or D in turn. Select the class’s answer, then press Submit. Explain the reasoning briefly. Do not advance until the discussion is finished.

audience.question: Resolution 18-NQ/TW (2017) sets the principle that an agency may handle many tasks, but each task should have one lead agency with main responsibility. Three offices now review the same permit application, and each waits for the others. Which arrangement best follows this principle?

options.text: Keep the three reviews running in parallel and combine the opinions at the end.
Name one office as lead with main responsibility, and have the others coordinate through it.
Merge the three offices into one but keep the same three review steps.
Ask the applicant to coordinate between the offices and report any conflicts.

assessment.explanation: Resolution 18-NQ/TW (25 October 2017) of the 12th Central Committee calls for a political system that is streamlined and works effectively and efficiently; it names overlapping functions and weak accountability among the problems to solve. Merging offices, running reviews in parallel or passing coordination to citizens does not make responsibility clear. The example is illustrative and does not show how far overlap has been reduced in practice.

presenter.script: We began with one question: how can reform help the system serve people better? A smaller structure is one step. Clear responsibility and accessible services must follow. Success depends on implementation and citizens’ experience. Our responsibility is to understand the evidence and explain it honestly. Thank you for listening.
